## A Life Between Two Lands

Born in the Belgian town of Mouscron, Rémy Cogghe was a child of movement and industry. When he was only thirteen, his father moved the family to France to seek work as a spinner in the industrial heart of Roubaix. It was here, amidst the rhythmic sounds of the textile mills, that the young boy first encountered the local Academy. This early exposure planted seeds of curiosity that would eventually lead him far beyond the factory walls.

His formal training took him to the École des Beaux-arts in 1876, where he studied under the guidance of Alexandre Cabanel. A curious complication arose during his pursuit of the prestigious Prix de Rome; while he was a candidate for the honor, it was discovered that his Belgian citizenship barred him from certain French recognitions. This setback led him back to Mouscron, where he sought lodgings and applied for the prize through the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp instead. His persistence bore fruit when he was awarded the prize in 1879, earning a gold medal for his painting, The Aduatuci Sold as Slaves.

## Travels and the Light of the South

With the success of his early accolades, Cogghe embarked on five years of extensive wandering. He moved through Spain and Italy, and even reached as far as Algeria and Tunisia. These travels were not merely for leisure but were periods of intense productivity. He painted prolifically, absorbing the varied landscapes and cultures he encountered along the way. The light of the Mediterranean and the North African coast surely left its mark on his eye.

By 1885, the wanderlust subsided, and he returned to Roubaix to live with his parents. He was a man who built his own stability; by 1893, his success allowed him to construct his own house in the town that had shaped his youth. His work began to settle into a focus on the people and the rhythms of the region.

Rémy Cogghe, originally spelled Rémi Coghe [1] ( 31 October 1854 – 2 April 1935) was a Belgian-born painter, residing in France.

## Biography

He was born in Mouscron. When he was thirteen, his father moved the family to France to take a job as a spinner in the industrial town of Roubaix. [1] He took his first art lessons at the local Academy. In 1876, he entered the École des Beaux-arts, where he studied under Alexandre Cabanel. Four years later, he was a candidate for the Prix de Rome, but it was discovered that he was still a Belgian citizen, so he returned to Mouscron, took temporary lodgings and applied for the Prix de Rome (Belgium) from the Royal Academy of Fine Arts (Antwerp). [1] He was awarded the prize in 1879 and received a gold medal for his painting The Aduatuci Sold as Slaves. [2] 

Cogghe spent the next five years travelling extensively throughout Spain and Italy, with visits to Algeria and Tunisia, painting prolifically all the way. In 1885, he returned to Roubaix and moved in with his parents. [1] By 1893, he had become successful enough that he could afford to build his own house. He specialized in portraits, but also painted scenes from the daily life of Roubaix and the surrounding region. Between 1879 and 1926, he exhibited in the foreign section at the Salon twenty-nine times.

Cogghe died on 2 April 1935 in Roubaix.

Rémy Cogghe, originally spelled Rémi Coghe ( 31 October 1854 – 2 April 1935) was a Belgian-born painter, residing in France.
## Biography
He was born in Mouscron. When he was thirteen, his father moved the family to France to take a job as a spinner in the industrial town of Roubaix. He took his first art lessons at the local Academy. In 1876, he entered the École des Beaux-arts, where he studied under Alexandre Cabanel. Four years later, he was a candidate for the Prix de Rome, but it was discovered that he was still a Belgian citizen, so he returned to Mouscron, took temporary lodgings and applied for the Prix de Rome (Belgium) from the Royal Academy of Fine Arts (Antwerp). He was awarded the prize in 1879 and received a gold medal for his painting The Aduatuci Sold as Slaves.
Cogghe spent the next five years travelling extensively throughout Spain and Italy, with visits to Algeria and Tunisia, painting prolifically all the way. In 1885, he returned to Roubaix and moved in with his parents. By 1893, he had become successful enough that he could afford to build his own house. He specialized in portraits, but also painted scenes from the daily life of Roubaix and the surrounding region. Between 1879 and 1926, he exhibited in the foreign section at the Salon twenty-nine times.

Biography

[ edit ]
He was born in Mouscron . When he was thirteen, his father moved the family to France to take a job as a spinner in the industrial town of Roubaix . [ 1 ] He took his first art lessons at the local Academy. In 1876, he entered the École des Beaux-arts , where he studied under Alexandre Cabanel . Four years later, he was a candidate for the Prix de Rome , but it was discovered that he was still a Belgian citizen, so he returned to Mouscron, took temporary lodgings and applied for the Prix de Rome (Belgium) from the Royal Academy of Fine Arts (Antwerp) . [ 1 ] He was awarded the prize in 1879 and received a gold medal for his painting The Aduatuci Sold as Slaves . [ 2 ]
Cogghe spent the next five years travelling extensively throughout Spain and Italy, with visits to Algeria and Tunisia, painting prolifically all the way. In 1885, he returned to Roubaix and moved in with his parents. [ 1 ] By 1893, he had become successful enough that he could afford to build his own house. He specialized in portraits, but also painted scenes from the daily life of Roubaix and the surrounding region. Between 1879 and 1926, he exhibited in the foreign section at the Salon twenty-nine times.
Cogghe died on 2 April 1935 in Roubaix.

Mouscron, 1854 - Roubaix/France, 1935
Peintre de scènes de genre, de portraits et de paysages. Son père, un ouvrier journalier originaire de la région de Roulers, est venu s'établir à Mouscron, comme tisserand, avant 1846, pour ensuite exercer le métier de boucher à Roubaix. Cogghe fréquente d'abord l'école académique de Roubaix, dirigée par C. Mils, où il obtient une médaille de vermeil en 1873. Cette académie lui décerne le grand prix de Rome pour la peinture en 1880. Entre 1881 et 1885, le peintre séjourne, en tant que boursier, successivement à Paris, Rome, Tolède et Florence. Il se fixe à Roubaix et se manifeste, de 1885 à 1935, par des envois annuels au Salon des Artistes français à Paris. S'il exécute des portraits sur commande, d'une facture souvent conventionnelle, il demeure essentiellement un peintre académique, témoin de la réalité quotidienne, populaire ou bourgeoise, de son temps.

Rémy Cogghe, originally spelled Rémi Coghe ( 31 October 1854 – 2 April 1935) was a Belgian-born painter, residing in France.
## Biography
He was born in Mouscron. When he was thirteen, his father moved the family to France to take a job as a spinner in the industrial town of Roubaix. He took his first art lessons at the local Academy. In 1876, he entered the École des Beaux-arts, where he studied under Alexandre Cabanel. Four years later, he was a candidate for the Prix de Rome, but it was discovered that he was still a Belgian citizen, so he returned to Mouscron, took temporary lodgings and applied for the Prix de Rome (Belgium) from the Royal Academy of Fine Arts (Antwerp). He was awarded the prize in 1879 and received a gold medal for his painting The Aduatuci Sold as Slaves.
Cogghe spent the next five years travelling extensively throughout Spain and Italy, with visits to Algeria and Tunisia, painting prolifically all the way. In 1885, he returned to Roubaix and moved in with his parents. By 1893, he had become successful enough that he could afford to build his own house. He specialized in portraits, but also painted scenes from the daily life of Roubaix and the surrounding region. Between 1879 and 1926, he exhibited in the foreign section at the Salon twenty-nine times.
